evidence_quote: 水系 deep eutectic electrolytes（DEE）对低成本锌离子电池很有潜力，但现有体系的性能往往有限，因此发现新的电解质体系非常重要，却又耗时耗资源。本文提出一个基于大语言模型的 multi-agent network，用于为锌离子电池提出新的 DEE 组成方案。该系统通过分析 DEE 相关学术文献，识别能够与 Zn(BF4)2·xH2O 配对的创新、低成本、可持续 Lewis bases。作者得到一个 Zn(BF4)2·xH2O-ethylene carbonate (EC) 体系，表现出较高电导率（10.6 mS cm−1）和较宽电化学稳定窗口（2.37 V）。优化后的电解质支持稳定的 zinc stripping/plating，在 Zn||polyaniline 电池中达到较好的倍率性能并支持 4000 次循环。光谱分析和模拟进一步揭示，EC 与 Zn2+ 的配位有助于抑制水致腐蚀，并形成富氟 hybrid organic/inorganic SEI，从而提升稳定性。整体上，这是一个从文献知识到材料组成建议再到实验验证的 LLM 驱动材料发现案例。

primary_source_excerpt:
Recent studies have started to explore AI agents for cosmology and scientific discovery 1,2,3,
with early demonstrations on realistic cosmological tasks such as weak-lensing analyses 4. In-
spired by the work on self-evolving agents 5, we discuss two complementary agentic AI systems
that can be applied to scientific discovery in cosmology: one for quantitative tasks with ex-
plicit evaluation metrics, and one for more open-ended scientific workflows. We present our
preliminary results on cosmological applications of our algorithms.
2
Multi-agent systems for scientific discovery
We review the fundamental concepts of AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery. Formally,
an agent A can be modelled as the tuple A = (L, C, τ), where L is the LLM backbone, C is
the context information received, and τ is the tools available for a single agent. Agents solve
problems through multi-agent collaboration. Given a research problem and a dataset D, the
agentic system initiates a high-level goal G, and then follows a policy π to generate a sequence of
actions {a0, . . . , aN} that execute a collection of sub-procedures aimed at advancing the system
towards the solution. The policy may be viewed as a conditional probability distribution over
actions given the high-level goal G, the available tools T , and the context Ct−1 before the decision
step t, such that
at ∼π(· | G, T , Ct−1).
(1)
Autonomous scientific discovery may be formulated as the problem of finding a solution that
maximizes the expected utility of a discovery trajectory. Let
Ξ0:N = (C0, a0, O1, C1, . . . , aN, ON+1, CN+1)
denote the trajectory generated by the agentic system, where Ot represents the observation, tool
output, or experimental result obtained during the discovery process. The system seeks a policy
π∗, such that
π∗= arg maxπ EΞ0:N∼π[U(Ξ0:N; G, D)] .
(2)
Here, U is a task-dependent utility function over the discovery trajectory.
In quantitative
settings, it may be defined by explicit metrics, such as parameter recovery or agreement with
data.
In more open-ended settings, it may instead reflect broader scientific value, such as
generating hypotheses, identifying unexpected patterns, or proposing interpretable explanations.
3
Methodology
We consider the two settings for agentic scientific discovery introduced in Sec. 2: closed tasks
with explicit quantitative objectives, and open-ended scientific workflows with only partially
specified goals.
3.1
CMBEvolve: automated algorithm discovery through LLM-guided tree search
For tasks with explicit quantitative metrics, we use an algorithmic evolution approach to find
the optimal solution. We present CMBEvolve a, a package for automated scientific code evolution
through LLM-guided tree search. Given a task for which the candidate solutions can be evaluated
by a score s, we represent the search process as a rooted tree T = (V, E), where V is the set
of nodes and E the parent-child edges.
Each node belongs to one of the four types: task,
idea generation and selection, code generation, and code mutation. Each node stores search
statistics used by the selection rules, including best score S∗and visit count N, together with
the corresponding generated content and execution outputs. After code evaluation, the score
assigned to a node is backpropagated from that node to the root, updating the statistics of all
ancestor nodes. The general workflow of CMBEvolve is illustrated in Fig. 1(a).

c. Grounded Feedback as the Foundation for Reliable MCTS Exploration
A decisive factor for successful long-horizon iteration is obtaining correct feedback signals,
since the guidance for refinement and expansion is essential. In the MCTS Exploration of
PHYSMASTER, RAG-Based factual feedback is produced by the supervisor as a critic: it (i)
assigns scalar rewards, (ii) determines the types of subsequent nodes, (iii) summarizes the
current exploration state to preserve the minimal information needed and (iv) actionable critique
to guide next step. The information above are fed back into the tree policy to guide subsequent
selection and expansion.
d. MCTS for Broad and Diverse Exploration
During tree search, nodes are selected using UCT (Upper Confidence bounds applied to
Trees) scores, and the structured search tree is expanded iteratively. The UCT value for a node 𝑣
is calculated as:

MCTS provides a principled mechanism to (i) exploit high-reward partial solutions, while (ii)
continuing to explore under-investigated alternatives to avoid premature convergence. This tree-
structured exploration is especially beneficial in long-horizon settings because the search tree
itself serves as an externalized record of diverse trajectories. By prioritizing under-explored paths
through UCT and supporting parallel multi-trajectory expansion, MCTS enhances efficiency
and scalability in navigating vast solution spaces typical of physics problems.

2 Results
In cold-atoms based quantum sensors, dense cold-atoms source at sub-µK tempera-
tures is typically required for improving sensing precision and sensitivity. To achieve
this, the experimental process is divided into two stages: capturing and cooling the
atomic ensemble to the sub-mK level using a magneto-optical trap (MOT), followed
by further reducing the temperature to the µK level through sub-Doppler cooling.
As illustrated in Fig. 1c, our experimental platform combines commercially available
lasers with self-developed control systems. First, we stabilize the laser frequency using
modulation transfer spectroscopy and optical phase-locked loop. Then, three pairs of
circularly polarized orthogonal lasers, along with a gradient magnetic field, form a
MOT for cooling and trapping rubidium atoms within the vacuum chamber. In our
system, polarization gradient cooling (PGC) serves as the primary mechanism for sub-
Doppler cooling. The advantage of this approach is its simplicity, as it does not require
any additional optical or electronic components. After loading the MOT, the magnetic
field is turned off after 1s, and the laser frequency and power are adjusted accordingly.
To determine the total number of atoms in the MOT, we use pixel integration from
charge coupled device (CCD) images, as shown in Fig. 2b. This step aims to acquire a
dense atomic cloud. During the PGC stage, we employ the molasses diffusion method
to measure the temperature and atom number. Representative images are shown in
Fig. 2e, while the fitted results of the atomic cloud diffusion radius are presented
below. Our objective is to obtain a cold atomic ensemble with plenty of atoms.
The whole experiments are subject to significant uncertainties. Controllable vari-
ables, such as optical parameters, dictate the upper limit of optimization during the
tuning process, while uncontrollable variables, such as environmental factors, restrict
the system’s generalization capabilities. Given the high-dimensional and sparse nature
of the parameters, combined with the substantial experimental costs, researchers must
carefully balance cost and performance. This often renders parameter selection heavily
reliant on prior experimental experience. Furthermore, manual optimization is limited
in its ability to simultaneously consider multiple objectives, significantly increasing the
complexity of the process. The intricate experimental procedure and time-consuming
individual sub-experiments optimizations limit the total number of trials that can be
performed. The quality of the atomic cloud produced in the cooling stage directly
influences key outcomes such as the signal-to-noise ratio of interference signals.
2.1 Adaptive optimization

regarding the list of sub-experiments, their order, and specific requirements. The Deci-
sion Maker calls the Experimenter sequentially according to the sub-experiment order.
Based on the requirements of different sub-experiments, the Experimenter automati-
cally selects appropriate optimization methods and sets experimental parameters using
retrieval-augmented generation to retrieve hardware parameter reports from a knowl-

Technical Feasibility (Tf) : This dimension validates the
maturity and implementability of process technologies, eval-
uating reaction mechanism rationality, separation technol-
ogy applicability, and operational control complexity.
Topological Rationality (Tr) : This metric evaluates the
completeness and optimization degree of process topology,
including unit operation connectivity logic and material ﬂow
rationality to verify efﬁcient process structure design. The
overall evaluation score for each iteration is computed as a
weighted combination of the individual dimensions.

Enhanced MCTS
Inspired by AFlow(Zhang et al. 2024b), our Enhanced
Monte Carlo Tree Search(E-MCTS) approach aims to ad-
dress a critical limitation in iterative search processes, where
conﬁgurations that fail to converge are often overlooked de-
spite containing valuable design insights worthy of further
exploration. In E-MCTS structure, each tree node repre-
sents a complete process conﬁguration rather than individual
unit operations, enabling the exploration of diverse complex
chemical process designs.
Initialization E-MCTS begins with three initial nodes
generated by workﬂow, derived from the user’s input, serv-
ing as the foundation for systematic exploration. The root
node is created as a virtual node, with the three initial conﬁg-
urations becoming its child nodes. We initialize the dynamic
candidate pool as an empty set and establish key parameters,
including the dynamic weight α(0) for initial exploration fo-
cus and the exploration coefﬁcient c(0).
Selection with Dual-Layer Value Evaluation We pro-
pose a dual-layer value evaluation system to address the
unique challenge where failed conﬁgurations may contain
valuable design insights. Our approach distinguishes be-
tween immediate value (derived directly from simulation
scores) and potential value (considering multi-dimensional
metrics). For failed conﬁgurations, we recognize exceptional
performance in speciﬁc dimensions as indicators of reﬁne-
ment potential. The combined value integrates both perspec-
tives through dynamic weighting:
V (ni, t) = α(t) · Vimm(ni) + (1 −α(t)) · Vpot(ni)

exploration-focused

enhance node selection by incorporating domain-speciﬁc
features, augmenting the standard UCB formula:
UCBenh(ni, t) = Vcomb(ni, t) + c(t)

where the feature weighting function Ψ(ni) incorporates

measures, and depth preferences.
Expansion During the expansion phase, each selected
node generates three child conﬁgurations. We execute a new
workﬂow iteration to update conﬁgurations, leveraging both
the selected node’s conﬁguration and historical insights from
past iterations. The experience encompasses all modiﬁca-
tions with their corresponding improvements or failures,
along with precise logs of predictions and expected outputs,
maximizing insight extraction from previous attempts.
Dynamic Revisit Mechanism In contrast to traditional
MCTS which abandons low-scoring branches, we maintain
a dynamic candidate pool containing the second and third
highest-scoring nodes that have not been revisited. When
global improvement stagnates, the algorithm selects nodes
for revisitation based on the gap between potential and real-
ized performance:
nrev = arg max

This mechanism prevents premature convergence and en-
ables the algorithm to escape local optima by revisiting
promising conﬁgurations that initially failed due to subop-
timal parameters.
Terminal Conditions We implement comprehensive ter-
mination criteria tailored to chemical process optimiza-
tion: (1) discovery of conﬁgurations exceeding target per-
formance, (2) reaching iteration limits, (3) global improve-
ment stagnation across all active leaves, or (4) high conver-
gence indicated by concentrated visit frequencies and sta-
ble scores. The ﬁnal solution selection combines solution
quality (70% weight), search conﬁdence as measured by
visit frequency (20% weight), and stability indicators (10%
weight), ensuring robust and reliable process conﬁgurations.
This E-MCTS algorithm effectively addresses the chal-
lenges of chemical process optimization by recognizing
value in failed conﬁgurations, dynamically balancing explo-
ration and exploitation, and implementing intelligent revisit
strategies to systematically navigate the vast design space.
Experiment
Baselines
We evaluate our approach against four categories of base-
lines: (1) End-to-end methods: We prompt GPT-4o and
Claude Sonnet 4 to directly generate JSON request con-
ﬁgurations. (2) Multi-agent workﬂows: We employ Swarm,
AutoGen, CrewAI, MetaGPT to benchmark our multi-agent
workﬂow’s effectiveness. (3) Human expert baseline: We
invite three chemical engineering experts to perform man-
ual design and computational validation. (4) Our methods:
We evaluate two variants of our proposed approach—a base
workﬂow without thermodynamic analysis workﬂow and an
enhanced version incorporating thermodynamic analysis.

This ensures that the generated questions are directly actionable and

(2) Tool execution and answer generation: Once the questions are 
generated, we proceed to tool execution and answer generation by 
utilizing the ReACT framework in conjunction with GPT-4o. ReACT21 has 
demonstrated its effectiveness in handling a limited number of tools. 
Therefore, only the tools relevant to the question are fed to ReACT, 
improving the accuracy of tool invocation.
(3) Manual review: The final step involves manual review to ensure 
the quality of generated answers. We invite three domain-specific 
experts to meticulously review the questions, tool usage and answers 
to verify their correctness and significance.
Finally, SciToolEval consists of 531 questions associated with the 
required tools and their corresponding answers. These questions cover 
single and multiple tools for problem-solving, and they are catego-
rized into different levels based on difficulty: Level-1 involves simple 
information queries using a single tool; Level-2 includes sequential 
and parallel use of multiple tools, requiring basic planning, reasoning 
and summarization skills. More details of the dataset construction are 
presented in Supplementary Section 2.
Implementation of SciToolAgent
SciToolAgent’s architecture revolves around three core components 
powered by LLMs: Planner, Executor and Summarizer (Fig. 1c). Each 
component plays a distinct role in the problem-solving workflow by 
leveraging the strengths of LLMs.
Planner. The Planner is responsible for devising a strategy to solve 
the given query. It leverages LLMs to interpret the question, query 
the SciToolKG and generate a plan of the chain of tools. Specifically, 
a retrieve-augmented generation approach based on the SciToolKG 
is proposed to identify and sequence the appropriate tools needed. 
The process begins with the LLM querying the SciToolKG based on the 
input question, followed by the steps described below.
(1) Full-graph retrieval: We first retrieve the most relevant k tools 
for the given question in the full graph of SciToolKG. This is achieved 
by calculating the semantic similarity between the question and all 
of the triples involved in tool functions within the SciToolKG. The 
similarity score helps in identifying tools that are most likely to be 
useful for the given query. Mathematically, let Ti represent a tool in

Executor. The Executor aims to ensure the effective implementation 
of the planned chain of tools. This component is designed to handle 
tool inputs, manage execution processes and address any errors that 
may arise during execution. It also integrates a robust safety module 
to monitor and control potentially hazardous inputs or outputs. The 
execution process involves the four steps as follows.
(1) Input preparation: The Executor uses LLMs to extract the 
required input parameters for the current tool in the chain. This involves 
parsing the question, understanding the context and identifying the 
necessary data to feed into the tool. Inputs are formatted accord-
ing to the specifications of the tool recorded in SciToolKG. This may 
include converting data types, structuring the input in a specific 
format or integrating multiple inputs.
(2) Tool execution: The Executor invokes the tool with the prepared 
inputs, which involves interfacing with the tool’s API. The execution 
process is actively monitored to track progress, capture outputs and 
detect any anomalies or errors. The Executor logs execution details to 
ensure traceability. Once the tool has been executed, the outputs are 
captured and further processed as needed to be compatible with the 
subsequent tools in the chain.
(3) Error handling and retries: The Executor is equipped with 
protocols to detect errors during tool execution. Errors can occur 
due to incorrect inputs, tool malfunctions or other unforeseen issues. 
When an error is detected, the Executor adjusts the inputs on the basis 
of predefined rules or heuristics to rectify the issue.

Computing scan paths via inverse optimization. Flows move particles into alignment 
with the specified objective. Using the cost function generated by the language 
model, the optimizer autonomously selects scan paths. (a) 7 linear scan paths are 
selected and overlapped to arrange 20 particles as a circle. Here the optimization 
relies on SLSQP operating over a precomputed lookup-table (LUT) flow model, 
where each of the N = 7 scan paths contributes three parameters (position, 
orientation, amplitude), yielding a 21-dimensional optimization problem. The effective 
control field emerges as the superposition of the individual sub-flows, producing 
complex yet physically consistent actuation patterns from mathematically grounded 
primitives. (b) Cost metric of circle versus time in simulation steps. (c-e) 
Demonstration of actuation-agnostic alignment capabilities.  Laser scan paths are 
shown in top right corners. (c) The actuation pattern is switched to a circular flow 
field to align four particles as a square after 8 steps of the simulation. (d) The 
actuation pattern is switched to a “saddle point” flow field and achieves alignment in

alignment, here at time step 10.

4. Local first pass execution. The chemistry engine tests the LLM’s first plan by turning
it into real route proposals. It enforces synthetic validity, removes duplicate routes, scores

5. LLM reflective revision. The LLM is shown what happened and is asked to improve
its plan before the iteration finishes. It uses the first pass outcome summary to revise the
strategy for the remaining candidate budget.
6. Local second pass execution and selection. The revised plan is tested in the same
chemistry pipeline, and the best candidates from both passes are kept.
The pooled
candidates are ranked by the task score, then committed to the island population, archive,
and memory.
7. LLM learning report. Finally, the LLM writes down the lesson from the iteration so
that the next iteration does not start from scratch. A compact report of useful strategies,
reaction patterns, motifs, and failure modes is carried forward to guide the next iteration.
Thus, the LLM remains a planner and reviewer, while route construction, validation, scoring,
deduplication, and population updates remain deterministic local operations.

different, which we term calibrated deference: the capacity to recognize when
its own tools or assumptions are failing, to adapt its strategy in response, and
to generate mechanistic hypotheses that guide experimental revision. We tested
CLIO in a closed-loop human–AI campaign to design an aqueous organic redox

Figure 2: Contextual modulation of KRAS repair efficacy stratified by clinical status. Boxplot analysis showing the 
differential sensitivity delta of in silico KRAS repair in MSI-High versus MSS cell line backgrounds. 
 
In silico CRISPR screening identifies the KRAS Shield and PIK3CA Paradox 
 
We performed a population-scale inverse-reasoning loop across unique genomic perturbations (Figure 3). Because our 
model captures the causal logic of the tumour microenvironment, it functions as an invertible simulator. We deployed an 
autonomous LLM Agent to conduct an in silico CRISPR screen across the cohort, querying the mathematical model to 
determine how repairing specific oncogenes would impact drug sensitivity. The neuro-symbolic agent correctly identified 
a major pivot in the biological logic. Contrary to classical, APC-centric models of CRC initiation, the agent identified 
mutant KRAS as the dominant driver of 5-FU resistance (Δ = -0.0469). The reasoning layer mapped this resistance to a 
"KRAS Shield", an active blockade mediated by downstream MAPK and PI3K network dependencies that prevents 
5-FU cytotoxicity. 
 
Furthermore, the agent autonomously deduced the "PIK3CA Paradox". While PIK3CA is a known oncogenic driver, the 
simulator revealed that repairing it paradoxically increases tumour resistance to 5-FU (Δ = +0.0085). Rather than 
attributing this to random noise, the neuro-symbolic agent logically reasoned that the PI3K and MAPK pathways 
maintain a compensatory relationship. In this specific cohort, inhibiting the PI3K pathway via in silico repair triggers a 
feedback loop that hyperactivates the more dominant KRAS/MAPK survival pathway, ultimately strengthening the cell's 
ability to withstand 5-FU-induced apoptosis.

On the other hand, the mixing or processing of the starting materials can be done on this 
platform. With this integration of automated chemistry labs (SDL), the laboratory of the future 
will be fully automated, becoming a plug-and-play chemistry environment. Scalable synthesis 
will combine AI/ML for planning and robotics for implementation and production.61,82–94 
 
More workflows will be tied to reinforcement learning (RL), a subset of ML. The RL can be 
implemented by taking the current state of the system, inferring which changes (some 
trial-and-error allowed) have occurred, and designing a response. It is compatible with 
multi-step processes as it makes decisions with each step and predicts a future response. In 
telescoping reactions or in planning multi-step and tandem protocols, RL will be beneficial for a 
closed-loop SDL experimentation.  It can learn to be efficient with materials and time, with each 
termination or failure yielding more data. In a recent workshop sponsored by the U.S. 
Department of Energy and Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the future of self-driving 
autonomous laboratories and the many aspects of SDL were mapped for future needs and 
implementation.95

At the start of one research round, OR-Agent allows temporary performance degradation when
exploring new research directions. Child nodes are not required to outperform the root or previous
elite immediately, reflecting the reality that early experiments along a novel direction may initially
underperform. Termination decisions are instead governed by sustained lack of improvement, controlled
via configurable parameters.
Context Engineering for Tree Awareness.
When expanding a node in the research tree and
generating child ideas, different strategies can be adopted for constructing the input context provided
to the Lead Agent. In particular, OR-Agent supports multiple levels of contextual scope: i) including
only the immediate parent node; ii) including the full ancestry path from the root to the current node;
iii) including the entire research tree to provide a global view of the ongoing research process. OR-Agent
exposes these options as configurable choices and, by default, adopts the third strategy, enabling the
Lead Agent to maintain global situational awareness over the research landscape. This design allows
the agent to reason not only about local refinements but also about the overall exploration–exploitation
balance across the tree. The serialization format used by OR-Agent is illustrated in Figure 3.
Figure 4 provides an illustrative example of multiple research rounds, showing how the size and
shape of the research tree evolve dynamically over time. Promising research directions are explored
more deeply, while unproductive branches are pruned. Although many high-quality solutions originate
from elite parent nodes, the figure also highlights that valuable discoveries can emerge from non-elite
starting points, underscoring the importance of maintaining sufficient exploratory breadth.

tiple reformulated queries can substantially enhance retrieval coverage and downstream reasoning
quality. Moreover, RAG has recently been applied in the geospatial domain to support knowledge
discovery and contribute to downstream tasks such as spatial reasoning (Yu et al., 2025). However,
to the best of our knowledge, no prior work has leveraged RAG to extract geospatial knowledge
specifically for geospatial model construction, leaving an important gap for integrating structured
geographic knowledge into model design.
3
GEOEVOLVE
GeoEvolve is designed to automate geospatial model discovery by integrating evolutionary code
generation with structured geospatial knowledge. Unlike general-purpose code agents, GeoEvolve
incorporates domain-specific knowledge from spatial modeling literature and classical algorithms,
enabling the discovery of geospatial algorithms. Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework of Geo-
Evolve. It consists of four main components: (1) a code evolver, (2) an evolved code analyzer, (3)
a geospatial knowledge retriever, and (4) a geo-informed prompt generator. Together, these compo-
nents orchestrate a closed-loop process of code generation, evaluation, and refinement, leading to
the emergence of geospatial model discovery.
3.1
CODE EVOLVER
The central engine of GeoEvolve is the code evolver, an evolutionary coding agent that generates and
iteratively refines candidate algorithms. Beginning with an initial algorithm, the evolver performs
a fully autonomous pipeline of mutation, evaluation, and selection relying on the power of LLMs.
Candidate algorithms are represented as a group of executable code fragments. Mutations can be
parameter changes, operator substitutions, or structure modifications to the algorithm. Abstractly,
given a task-specific objective function L, the evolver seeks to optimize an algorithm A such that

As mentioned previously, the basic attributes used

scale, orientation, and form), texture (parameters fab-

and composition (parameters color, albedo, specular-
ity, and mineralogy). All these attribute parameters
can be expressed as discrete constants or modeled as
multivalued functions to reﬂect a variety of the real-
world situations (“vitreous luster”) and consequent
uncertainty.
For this study, a feature database of commonly
used parameters in terrestrial ﬁeld geology was com-
piled for each basic attribute, with each assigned an
arbitrary science value score (SVS) based on relative
geological signiﬁcance. Each target could be assessed
and described using the elements from a set of possi-
ble parameters for each attribute. Once the appropri-
ate parameters were identiﬁed for each target, their
scores, deﬁned in the database, could be used to build
up a cumulative score for each attribute. At the at-
tribute level, therefore, the accumulated scores repre-
sent indicators of “feature richness.” The overall SVS
of a science target is derived by combining all the fea-
tures observed/measured, expressed as parameters
for each attribute, and making adjustments based on
data quality and context (knowledge of the geological
environment in which the robot explores). At the start
of the mission, a contextual model would be primed
using prelanding data (regional geology from orbital
mapping) and mission objective criteria (search for
signatures of life). Following landing, the contextual
model would be enhanced using ground truth from
panoramic landing site surveys and in situ analytical
measurements.

factor.

primary_source_excerpt:
for routine experimental processes. AI Scientist agents [13, 11, 14, 7, 9, 10, 15] tackle the exploration challenge by
autonomously generating and evaluating novel hypotheses (e.g., the relationship between a certain mutation
and a certain disease) through integrated literature search, data analysis, and academic writing capabilities.
Our work embarks on a diﬀerent and more ambitious goal in scientiﬁc discovery: building agents to discover
new hypotheses to complex scientiﬁc design challenges, such as better therapeutic molecules and new func-
tional materials. This problem is uniquely challenging due to the “creativity” and “novelty” required and the
inﬁnite combinatorial search space for hypotheses. Previous work has sought to address these challenges by
developing optimization models that automatically ﬁnd hypotheses maximizing a manually deﬁned set of
quantitative objectives, such as drug eﬃcacy, protein expression, and material stability. These approaches,
ranging from traditional generative models to more recent LLM-based methods, have demonstrated the
ability to eﬃciently optimize against ﬁxed objectives in domains including drug design [16, 17, 18], algorithm
discovery [6], and materials design [19, 20].
However, these optimization models operate under a critical assumption: that the right set of objectives is
known upfront. In practice, this assumption seldom holds true a priori. Just as scientiﬁc discovery requires
iterations of hypothesis, experimentation, and observation, determining the appropriate objectives for a
discovery task is itself an iterative search process. Scientists must constantly tweak objectives based on
intermediate results, domain knowledge, and practical constraints that emerge during exploration (Figure 1(a)).
This iterative reﬁnement is particularly crucial in experimental disciplines such as drug discovery, materials
design, and protein engineering, where experimental success does not correlate well with computational
proxies [21, 22]. Without this evolving process, the discovery suﬀers from incomplete knowledge about the
design space: optimization algorithms exploit gaps between models and reality, producing solutions that
maximize predicted scores while missing important practical considerations that experts would recognize.
The search space for objectives and their relative weights is itself combinatorially large (Figure 1(b)), making
it extremely diﬃcult to specify the right objectives from the outset. As a result, while existing optimization
models can solve the low-level optimization problem eﬃciently, scientiﬁc discovery remains bottlenecked by
the high-level objective search process that relies on manual trial-and-error.
In this work, we introduce SAGA as our ﬁrst concrete step toward automating this iterative objective evolving
process. SAGA is designed to navigate the combinatorial search space of objectives by integrating high-level
objective planning in the outer loop with low-level optimization in the inner loop (Figure 1(c)). The outer
loop comprises four agentic modules: a planner that proposes new objectives based on the task goal and
current progress, an implementer that converts proposed objectives into executable scoring functions, an
optimizer that searches for candidate hypotheses maximizing the speciﬁed objectives, and an analyzer that
examines the optimization results and identiﬁes areas for improvement. Within the optimizer module, an
inner loop employs any optimization strategies (e.g., genetic algorithms or reinforcement learning-based
search) to iteratively evolve candidate hypotheses toward the current objectives. Importantly, SAGA is a
ﬂexible framework supporting diﬀerent levels of human involvement. It oﬀers three modes (Figure 1(d)):
(1) co-pilot mode, where scientists collaborate with both the planner and analyzer to reﬂect on results and
determine new objectives; (2) semi-pilot mode, where scientists provide feedback only to the analyzer; and
(3) autopilot mode, where both analysis and planning are fully automated. This design allows scientists to
interact with SAGA in ways that best suit their expertise and preferences.
We demonstrate SAGA as a generalist scientiﬁc discovery agentic framework with success across multiple
scientiﬁc domains, from chemistry and biology to materials science (Figure 1(e)-(f)). In antibiotic design, SAGA
identiﬁes a novel hit with experimentally validated antibacterial activity for E. coli, no cytotoxicity in human
cell lines, and a Tanimoto distance greater than 0.7 to all known antibiotics. In nanobody design, experimental
testing conﬁrms three de novo PD-L1 binders with KD ranging from 300nM to 400nM, and the composite
scoring function autonomously evolved by SAGA signiﬁcantly separates binders from non-binders (p = 0.03)

title: Beyond Execution: Auditing Experimental Fidelity in LLM-Driven Scientific Research

We ask AI agents to select and rank candidate training subsets that can be used to fine-tune a small LLM model. Agents are allowed to inspect the data, write and execute analysis code, and run model forward passes, but can not train the model or access the actual evaluation tasks. We then fine-tune the base model on each selected subset and evaluate its post-training performance under a standardized protocol. We instantiate the benchmark in terminal problem solving and tool use, selecting trajectories from OpenThoughts-Agent and EnvScaler and evaluating on TBLite and BFCL, respectively. We then evaluate the agents along two complementary dimensions: the post-training performance of the top-ranked subset, reflecting the ability to identify high-value training data, and ranking accuracy, reflecting the ability to predict the relative performance of the selected subsets. In our experiments, selection gains over random selection are limited; agents do not reliably rank their selected groups, and ranking ability does not hold consistently across tasks: Astra identifies the best group in all three tool-use runs but in only one of three terminal runs. We introduce MMPostTrainBench, a benchmark spanning eight tasks in image, audio, video, and joint audio-video understanding and image-grounded software repair. Evaluation covers target and non-target model outcomes, iterative model improvement and selection, and research integrity. Across all eight tasks, 52.1% of model–task means fall below the base, and evaluated submissions also exhibit non-target regressions. Model performance does not consistently improve across research iterations, and agents do not reliably select the best evaluated candidate for submission; final submissions trail that candidate by up to 5.38 percentage points. Extending autonomous research from text-only to multimodal tasks introduces additional sources of error in perception, cross-modal alignment, and temporal grounding. The observed regressions and selection gaps highlight the need to balance targeted improvements with non-target capability preservation and to retain gains across research iterations. These requirements motivate MMResearch, a multimodal research framework that connects media-grounded evidence to hypotheses and interventions, carries findings across rounds through hierarchical memory, and retains candidates using development evaluation. Added to existing code-agent runtimes, it improves submitted-model accuracy by up to 7.75 percentage points for Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code and 2.33 points for GPT-5.6-sol with Codex. | 高（一手正文；非独立复现） |

Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promise for such automation, yet their deployment in atmospheric governance remains constrained by limited access to real-time, heterogeneous environmental data and insufficient cross-disciplinary reasoning for comprehensive pollution analysis. Here we present Neuro-Air, an end-to-end multi-agent LLM framework that couples real-time air pollution data retrieval with a persistent code-execution sandbox. Built on a hierarchical architecture, a central coordinating agent directs five domain-specialized worker agents, emulating the thorough workflow of human experts in urban air pollution management. Across 317 real-world cases, Neuro-Air executed the full pipeline from heterogeneous data ingestion to structured output. In a matched ablation across five additional backbones, the multi-agent configuration achieved a pooled 88.4% accuracy on a common 90-task programmatically verified subset, scored against ground truth recomputed from the source data. Expert review further delineates an operating boundary, separating tasks where autonomous analysis is dependable from those requiring human judgement. Engineering Environmental sciences Image-Based Air Quality Estimation Using Deep Learning Techniques Introduction The dynamic complexity of atmospheric systems presents a fundamental challenge to urban air pollution management. The requisite synthesis of heterogeneous data and specialized domain expertise demands a level of real-time, interdisciplinary coordination that often exceeds current organizational capacities. For instance, on 26 November 2025, a large fire broke out in Hong Kong’s Tai Po district, and the ensuing 43 h combustion of building materials and foam panels across seven high-rise blocks released massive quantities of particulate matter and toxic pollutants into the local atmosphere 1 . During such acute events, local governments require precise, real-time pollution metrics and professional assessments for timely warnings and mitigation, while the general public simultaneously needs actionable advice to navigate the immediate health hazards. Comprehensively assessing these impacts, however, necessitates the integration of emission inventories, meteorological modeling, remote sensing data, chemical analyses, and health-risk assessment tools 2 , 3 , 4 . This is a highly complex procedure requiring teams of experts working for hours or days; moreover, the reliance on highly technical jargon creates a significant communication barrier for the general public, who urgently need accessible information without requiring professional expertise. These analytical workflows are challenging to orchestrate under tight timeframes, a difficulty that is acutely exacerbated in regions with limited technical expertise or monitoring infrastructure. In China, the imperative for effective management is particularly severe: an immense population suffers from PM2.5-related respiratory and cardiovascular conditions, with particulate matter contributing to over 1.42 million premature deaths annually and ranking as the fourth leading risk factor for mortality nationwide 5 , 6 . Although China maintains over 1700 national-level reference stations and thousands of provincial nodes, monitoring resources and analytical capacity remain unevenly distributed across regions 7 . This disparity creates a two-sided bottleneck in air quality management. In developed coastal agglomerations, the sheer volume and heterogeneity of monitoring data overwhelm existing expert capacity, resulting in analytical saturation. In western inland regions, by contrast, a shortage of skilled personnel and advanced analytical equipment means that even basic pollution analysis is frequently delayed, despite the availability of the underlying data 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 . Consequently, there is an urgent demand for an automated air pollution management system capable of performing complex analyses, presenting real-time data, and communicating with non-professional users. Such a system would provide critical support for both high-level decision-making and preliminary healthcare guidance, operating with less human intervention during the analytical phase, while preserving expert oversight for final policy decisions. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent reasoning capabilities 12 , 13 , 14 , motivating a gradual shift from passive text-processing instruments toward increasingly autonomous scientific assistants 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 . However, the deployment of monolithic LLMs in air pollution research is fundamentally constrained. Even in expert-level environmental science and engineering question answering, GPT-4 attains an expert-rated factuality of only 0.79, dropping below 0.5 on the most difficult items 20 . This unreliability becomes critical in autonomous scientific workflows, where agentic systems succeed precisely because generated programs are filtered by external execution and evaluation rather than trusted 21 , 22 . This reliability gap widens in complex technical domains, where mainstream models frequently fail to surpass 50% accuracy in intricate calculations or domain-specific modeling, which is a limitation that fine-tuning for environmental applications has not fully resolved 20 , 23 . Furthermore, while fine-tuning embeds specific domain knowledge, it often precipitates narrow specialization and overfitting 20 , 24 , precluding the interdisciplinary breadth necessary for holistic urban air pollution analysis. More critically, LLMs possess a fundamental architectural deficit regarding complex numerical analysis 25 , 26 , 27 . These limitations are exacerbated by the challenge of integrating heterogeneous, high-frequency data streams, which frequently induces context loss and catastrophic forgetting in information-dense environments. Yet, despite their inherent lack of numerical competence, LLMs have achieved strong proficiency in code generation, enabling the synthesis of executable algorithmic scripts from natural language prompts 28 , 29 , 30 . Our proposed framework directly builds upon this capability. In this work, we introduce Neuro-Air, a multi-agent framework designed to overcome these structural limitations by automating core procedures within the urban air pollution management cycle. Rather than proposing a new retrieval or execution algorithm, the architecture integrates two capabilities from our prior systems, domain-grounded knowledge retrieval and a persistent code-execution runtime, within a hierarchical multi-agent workflow, so that the analytical pipeline is decomposed across specialized agents instead of being handled by a single monolithic model 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 . To our knowledge, this is among the first end-to-end analytical workflows of this kind assembled for air pollution analysis. Unlike prior approaches in environmental engineering that address narrowly defined analytical tasks 24 , 35 , 36 , 37 , Neuro-Air encompasses the full spectrum of the management cycle. It integrates real-time air quality data, screens emission source-receptor associations, evaluates multi-dimensional impacts, and synthesizes candidate control strategies. We evaluated the framework using a dataset of 317 complex environmental queries drawn from two contrasting application settings: acute emergency response in Hong Kong SAR, a densely monitored coastal metropolis, and chronic industrial-emission analysis in Hebei, a heavily industrialized region within the well-instrumented Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei (BTH) air-quality coordination network. This validation utilized a rigorous human-in-the-loop protocol, cross-validating human expert assessments with autonomous AI Judges. To ensure methodological robustness, the framework was deployed across multiple mainstream LLM backbones to benchmark operational stability and consistency. Our results indicate that Neuro-Air mitigates several constraints of monolithic models on these tasks and provides a practical, reusable workflow for AI-assisted environmental analysis. The primary contributions of this work are threefold: Real-time assimilation of heterogeneous data: We establish an architectural protocol that integrates real-time, multimodal environmental data streams with semantic reasoning, designed to bridge the gap between raw sensor data and higher-level environmental analysis. Augmentation of LLM computational capacity: We augment foundation LLMs with algorithmic agents to mitigate their limitations in numerical reasoning and computation. This integration provides a foundation for executing complex atmospheric tasks, such as dynamic feature correlation and spatiotemporal analysis, that reside beyond the scope of monolithic models. Automation of interdisciplinary analytical workflows: We show that multi-agent collaboration can automate interdisciplinary analytical workflows that traditionally necessitate extensive human coordination, shortening the initial analytical synthesis and providing a scalable architecture to support environmental decision workflows. Ultimately, the framework serves as a decision-support tool for air quality management, with experts retaining responsibility for final judgments. It streamlines complex data integration and analytical workflows, thereby facilitating timely, data-driven regulatory action and public health protection. Results Functional overview and agent specialization A comprehensive urban air quality management lifecycle typically encompasses five core stages 38 : (1) objective identification, wherein governing institutions define policy thresholds, regulatory standards, and scientific baselines (e.g., acceptable pollutant concentrations or ozone formation mechanisms) through extensive literature and policy review; (2) pollution monitoring, which involves acquiring and processing high-resolution spatiotemporal data from sensor networks and satellite observations to establish early-warning systems and emergency analyses; (3) comprehensive assessment, requiring complex analytical procedures such as spatiotemporal distribution mapping, emission source-receptor association, meteorological factor analysis, and health risk evaluations; (4) strategy formulation, which translates complex analytical outputs into actionable mitigation strategies and accessible reports for non-expert stakeholders; and (5) continuous evaluation, ensuring ongoing monitoring of policy implementation and efficacy. To deploy LLMs across these interdisciplinary workflows, we built a suite of five domain-specific agents, structured into three functional modules: (i) External Knowledge and Data Extraction Agents (data pre-processing and knowledge retrieval); (ii) Analytical Agents (air pollution modeling and multi-variate analysis); and (iii) Synthesis and Communication Agents (visualization and report generation), as illustrated in Fig. 1 a. We used Claude 4 Sonnet 39 as the baseline backbone and benchmarked additional models (GPT-5 40 , Gemini 2.5 Pro 41 , DeepSeek-V3 42 ) in the evaluation below; each agent was initialized with a role-specific system prompt (shown in Table 2 ). Full size image a Multi-Agent Coordination: The framework integrates a central LLM coordinator with specialized environmental agents dedicated to data engineering, pollution analysis, and visualization; ( b ) Hierarchical Logic Layers: Three distinct operational layers govern the system: Role Definition (persona assignment), Task Execution (workflow management), and Compliance (quality and safety constraints); ( c ) Interactive User Interface: The Neuro-Air dashboard integrates a conversational chatbot with analytical outputs, translating complex datasets into interpretable, data-driven visualizations for non-professional stakeholders. To democratize access, we expose the pipeline through a natural-language web interface, enabling non-expert users such as government officials and the general public to use the system without domain knowledge or programming expertise (Fig. 1 c). A central LLM Coordinator interprets each query and decomposes it into step-wise subtasks using Chain-of-Thought 43 reasoning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation 44 , 45 , then orchestrates the specialized agents, each running under a role-defining prompt over the dual-stream runtime described below (configurations in Methods). In the final synthesis stage, the Coordinator consolidates the agents’ outputs into a coherent response, which may comprise textual analyses, quantitative summaries, visualizations, or policy recommendations. This work builds upon two of our previous studies. The first is AirGPT 46 , a domain-specific framework that integrates conversational AI with atmospheric science expertise. By drawing on a curated corpus of peer-reviewed literature and specialized data analysis tools, AirGPT addresses the outdated and fabricated information that limits general-purpose LLMs in air quality management. Figure 2 illustrates the complete external information and data retrieval process introduced in that work. The second is CaveAgent 47 , which employs a dual-stream architecture in which a persistent Python runtime, rather than the text context, serves as the central locus of state. By using the LLM as a runtime operator, this design enables the system to handle the complex computational problems. While AirGPT established the informational foundation (curated domain knowledge and external data pipelines) and CaveAgent provided the computational substrate (stateful Python runtime for numerical execution), neither system alone addresses the full complexity of urban air-pollution governance. AirGPT lacks autonomous computational capacity, as it retrieves and synthesizes information but cannot independently execute quantitative analyses. CaveAgent, conversely, provides execution capabilities but operates as a general-purpose runtime without domain-specialized analytical reasoning or multi-source data integration protocols. Neuro-Air’s contribution is the architectural integration of these complementary capabilities within a hierarchical multi-agent framework: it couples domain-grounded knowledge retrieval with autonomous computational execution, orchestrated by specialized agents that collectively span the entire pollution-management lifecycle. This integration enables end-to-end analyses that neither predecessor system supports on its own. Fig. 2: Illustration of Neuro-Air’s streamlined workflow for information retrieval. Dynamic pollution tracking and risk assessment during acute emission events To demonstrate Neuro-Air’s capacity for rapid response during emergent environmental crises, we evaluate its performance during the 2025 Hong Kong Urban Fire (Fig. 3 ). On November 26, 2025, a massive five-alarm fire broke out at the Wang Fuk Court housing complex in the Tai Po District of Hong Kong 48 . The system’s diagnostic workflow is initiated either autonomously, which is triggered by a continuous environmental monitoring daemon when local pollutant concentrations exceed predefined governmental thresholds, or via direct user query (e.g., “Assess the air quality impacts of the recent Tai Po fire"). It then translates these parameters into executable spatial-database queries, and the data-acquisition agent retrieves the nearest air-quality and meteorological stations within the influence zones. Following Algorithm 1, the system segments pollutant data into pre- and post-event phases to quantify short-term concentration spikes, correlates these spikes with meteorological conditions, and queries surrounding infrastructure for vulnerable receptors such as schools and hospitals, yielding a structured assessment of pollution severity, meteorological context, and proximity-based exposure. Within minutes of the event, the isolated execution environment flagged acute short-term anomalies at the nearest monitoring station during the first 24 h: peak PM 2.5 reached 54.6 μ g/m 3 (2.0 × the pre-fire mean) and peak NO 2 reached 123.2 μ g/m 3 (2.5 × the pre-fire mean). We emphasize that this output should be interpreted as a rapid, data-grounded screening signal that helps prioritize expert attention during an unfolding emergency, not as evidence of causation. The peak-to-mean ratio indicates the prominence of a short-term excursion but cannot, on its own, establish its cause, as similar peaks may arise from ordinary diurnal variability. The agent further cross-referenced the meteorological data and correctly noted that, despite the acute 24 h excursion, multi-day average pollution levels showed no sustained increase. Indeed, the station’s official AQHI remained within the moderate range (5–6) throughout the event. The system-generated meteorological summary reported a modal westerly wind component and a mean wind speed of 8.5 m/s based on 24 h aggregates. These results faithfully reflect the underlying database records; however, the westerly mode is driven largely by post-event observations, making the 24 h aggregation too coarse for event-specific interpretation. We therefore provide an hour-resolved expert reanalysis below while retaining the original system output verbatim in Supplementary Note 3 , together with an editorial note. Because the screening signal alone does not support causal attribution, we conducted the follow-up analyses specified by our governance framework: comparison against a matched historical baseline, a before-and-after network contrast using a difference-in-differences framework, and an interrupted-time-series-style analysis of the event-aligned hourly observations. First, a historical matched-hour baseline (the same station and clock hour over the preceding 14 days) shows the fire-evening NO 2 value (123.2 μ g/m 3 at 20:00) to be high but not unprecedented ( z = 1.9; the matched-hour maximum of the preceding fortnight was 125.5 μ g/m 3 on a non-fire evening), confirming that the raw peak-to-mean ratio overstates the anomaly. Second, a network contrast across all 18 general and roadside stations, in which the nearest station’s change against its own matched-hour baseline is differenced against the contemporaneous changes at control stations (a difference-in-differences reading), reveals that the same evening exhibited a territory-wide NO 2 elevation (mean rise of + 19.6 μ g/m 3 against matched hours; several stations far upwind of the fire rose as much as, or more than, the nearest station), coincident with hour-resolved observations of the northeast-monsoon flow weakening to near calm in the sheltered Tolo basin during the evening hours–conditions favouring general pollutant accumulation rather than a single-source plume. Third, the pollutant contrast most consistent with a local combustion contribution tells the most defensible story: in the evening network contrast the nearest station ranked first of 18 in PM 2.5 elevation ( + 7.4 μ g/m 3 above the network mean rise), a modest but direction-consistent local excess. The resulting synthesis is appropriately qualified yet operationally useful. The expert reanalysis indicates that the fire’s discernible local signature was a moderate elevation in particulate matter superimposed on a broader regional stagnation episode. The system’s minutes-scale screening appropriately prompted further investigation, whereas final attribution depended on expert-level reanalysis. This delineation of responsibilities reflects the human-AI division of labour underlying our framework. As part of the real-time workflow, the system complemented pollutant screening with a proximity-based indicator of potential exposure. It generated four concentric distance bands (0–500, 500–1000, 1000–1500, and 1500–2000 m) around the incident location and identified 293 residential buildings within 1.5 km, as well as 1090 buildings of all types within 2 km. The scope of interpretation, however, should be clearly delineated. In the absence of plume-direction, occupancy, and population data, these building counts indicate spatial proximity to the incident but do not quantify population exposure. Nevertheless, the analysis identified the Tai Po Baptist Public School, located approximately 35 m from the incident location, as a potentially sensitive receptor warranting priority expert review and consideration of targeted health communication. The synthesis and communication agent subsequently integrated these analytical outputs and generated visual summaries of the spatial distribution and temporal evolution of pollutant concentrations (Fig. 3 b–d). It then used the LLM’s semantic reasoning capabilities to translate the quantitative results into an accessible natural-language report for non-specialist stakeholders. A complete workflow and the generated answer can be found in Supplementary Note 3 . For emergency monitoring and early warning, the workflow provides two practical advantages over standalone LLMs. First, deterministic pipelines retrieve hourly observations directly from sensor networks, enabling near-real-time analysis without relying exclusively on the model’s static training knowledge. Second, the system grounds its analytical outputs in retrieved data and reproducible computations. Its visualizations, recommendations, and advisories are therefore traceable to the underlying evidence and analytical procedures, allowing experts to inspect and verify each stage of the analytical process. The following subsection details these capabilities and their Python-based implementation. Multi-variate emission analysis Beyond rapid emergency response, environmental management requires multi-variate analysis of the non-linear interactions among meteorology, traffic, and static geographical features such as topography and land use. To demonstrate this, we present an exploratory source-receptor association and emission-concentration screening case study of an iron smelting facility in Handan, Hebei (Fig. 4 ). Handan is a heavily industrialized priority city within the BTH air-quality coordination network. Its local analytical capacity, however, remains constrained by limited specialized expertise and advanced instrumentation, such that even routine air-quality assessments can require considerable time and manual effort. This setting complements the acute-event Hong Kong case by demonstrating the potential value of the framework in contexts with limited analytical resources. Fig. 4: Structured process-flow for Neuro-Air factory emission-concentration association screening. Full size image a Task initialization identifying factory coordinates and emission logs; ( b ) Geofenced screening of candidate receptor stations around the facility; ( c ) Python-based time-series analysis comparing emission fluctuations; ( d ) Evaluation of regulatory compliance, emission-concentration associations, and related metrics; ( e ) Synthesis of findings and automated report generation. In this scenario, Neuro-Air is tasked with analyzing carbon monoxide (CO) emissions from a large iron and steel facility in She County, Handan, Hebei, and evaluating their localized impact on ambient air quality from January 6 to 8, 2026 (Fig. 4 a). Upon receiving the query, the Central Coordinator orchestrates the analytical pipeline. Initially, the knowledge retrieval and data acquisition agents identify the facility’s spatial coordinates and extract the corresponding high-resolution emission logs and operational data. To identify which nearby monitoring stations are most strongly associated with the facility’s emissions, Neuro-Air autonomously geofences candidate receptor stations around the source and screens them by emission-concentration cross-correlation, rather than a physically calibrated dispersion model. By setting a 20 km geofencing radius, the agent retrieves synchronized ambient monitoring data from 18 surrounding stations. It then generates native Python code leveraging the SciPy library to compute the cross-correlation between the facility’s emission vectors and the ambient concentration signals (Fig. 4 b). Through this isolated execution, the system ranks the candidate receptors by association strength, identifying the Guxin Air Quality Station (located 12.2 km to the south of the facility) as the most strongly associated node, with a strong baseline correlation ( r = 0.77, p < 0.01). Algorithm 2 Autonomous source-receptor Association and Time-Lag Correlation To characterize the temporal association between facility emissions and ambient pollutant concentrations, the system calculated Pearson correlations over candidate lags of τ ∈ {0, …, 6} h. At Guxin, the maximum correlation occurred when concentrations were aligned with emissions recorded three hours earlier ( r = 0.83; Fig. 4 c). We interpret this as an empirical lag of maximum correlation, not a physically resolved transport time. Following Algorithm 2, the system then defined high- and low-emission periods using the 67th and 33rd percentiles of the emission distribution ( > 14, 288 and < 11, 857 kg/h, respectively). Under contemporaneous alignment, mean CO at Guxin was approximately 130% higher during high-emission hours than during low-emission hours (0.78 versus 0.34 mg/m 3 ), with a corresponding 16-point difference in mean AQI (Fig. 4 d). Because this comparison did not incorporate the identified three-hour lag, we repeated the analysis using lag-aligned observations. The association remained similar or slightly stronger: under the original thresholds, the difference in mean CO between high- and low-emission periods was + 0.46 mg/m 3 ( + 139%), accompanied by an 18-point difference in mean AQI. After recalculating the thresholds using the 69 lag-aligned pairs, the relative difference was + 134%. A moving-block bootstrap using 12-hour blocks and B = 10 4 replicates, with thresholds re-estimated in each replicate, yielded 95% intervals that excluded zero under both contemporaneous alignment ( + 0.20 to + 0.59 mg/m 3 ) and three-hour lag alignment ( + 0.24 to + 0.57 mg/m 3 ). The intervals remained bounded away from zero for block lengths of 6–24 h, indicating that the original difference between emission periods was not an artifact of temporal alignment. Nevertheless, these results represent statistical associations rather than causal effects and remain subject to the confounding factors discussed below. The system also generated targeted visualizations and a management-oriented synthesis (Fig. 4 e); the complete workflow and original response are provided in Supplementary Note 4 . Algorithm 2 summarizes the lag-consistent screening procedure used by Neuro-Air: it retrieves facility emission records and concentration measurements from nearby monitoring stations, evaluates candidate lags, identifies the lag of maximum correlation, retains associations that meet the predefined screening criterion, and compares concentrations between high- and low-emission periods under the selected temporal alignment. This analysis supports a statistical association between facility emissions and concentrations measured at Guxin, not a physically validated attribution of the observed pollution to the facility. Because the system’s meteorological query returned no wind records for the analysis window, its directional labels reflected only the geometric relationship between the facility and monitoring station; the wind field was therefore reconstructed independently by experts. Predominantly southwesterly winds prevailed and generally did not support direct transport from the facility to Guxin, which is located to its south. Shared diurnal cycles, regional background pollution, or emissions from other nearby facilities may therefore partly explain the observed correlation. Robust attribution is further limited by the short record ( ~ 72 hourly observations), temporal autocorrelation, shared meteorological forcing, and selection of the maximum correlation across 18 monitoring stations and 7 candidate lags. The r > 0.5 and p < 0.01 thresholds in Algorithm 2 should therefore be treated as descriptive screening criteria rather than formal inferential tests, particularly because the original procedure did not correct for the 126 comparisons arising from all combinations of stations and lags. As a post hoc sensitivity analysis, a Benjamini–Hochberg correction across all 126 comparisons retained the association between Guxin concentrations and facility emissions at a three-hour lag at a nominal false-discovery rate of 0.01 (unadjusted p = 7.3 × 10 −19 ). This correction, however, does not account for temporal dependence or environmental confounding. Moreover, 48 combinations involving 9 of the 18 monitoring stations met the original screening criteria, indicating a spatially diffuse pattern of correlations. This pattern is consistent with shared diurnal variation and regional background pollution rather than an association uniquely localized to Guxin. An independent companion analysis likewise did not support a physically credible transport relationship: the correlation was higher under winds unfavourable for transport from the facility to Guxin ( r = 0.777, n = 62) than under favourable winds ( r = 0.640, n = 8), although the small number of favourable-wind observations limits this comparison. The inconsistent physical interpretations obtained from the same data demonstrate that reliable code execution does not ensure stable source attribution and underscore the need for expert review. Regulatory use would require wind-resolved dispersion analysis, correction for multiple comparisons across monitoring stations and candidate lags, explicit treatment of temporal dependence and confounding, and validation using independent observations. A key factor underlying Neuro-Air’s effectiveness in this workflow is its dual-stream architecture, which decouples semantic reasoning from mathematical computation. General-purpose LLMs may produce unsupported outputs in pollution source attribution, such as selecting monitoring stations without sufficient scientific justification, and such limitations cannot be fully resolved by simply embedding physical equations in the prompt. Conversely, task-specific fine-tuned models may lack the flexibility required for changing analytical conditions. Neuro-Air addresses these limitations by using the LLM for logical orchestration and code generation while delegating numerical modeling to an isolated Python environment. This separation improves methodological transparency by allowing researchers to inspect generated scripts, intermediate outputs, and data logs for analytical validity and data provenance. For complex atmospheric analyses involving iterative and multi-step calculations, direct Python execution can also reduce repeated model calls and external tool interactions, thereby lowering latency, computational overhead, and token consumption. By transforming heterogeneous sensor data into actionable information, Neuro-Air bridges raw environmental observations and downstream decision-making, providing preliminary guidance on pollution conditions and associated health considerations. Evaluation of Neuro-Air’s performance We assembled a multi-source dataset (air quality, traffic, meteorological, geospatial, and emission data) for Hong Kong 49 , 50 , 51 , 52 , 53 , 54 and Hebei Province, and curated a benchmark of 317 representative queries (200 Hebei, 117 Hong Kong) drawn from practitioner interviews, official government documentation, and citizen inquiries 55 , 56 , 57 , 58 ; the two queries driving the case studies are held out and reported separately. The queries are stratified into six functional domains (Temporal Pattern, Geospatial, Multivariate Environmental, Urban Environmental Planning, Environmental Decision Support, and Personal Environmental Action Planning), collectively spanning spatio-temporal analysis, city-level planning, and management guidance. Full metadata and the benchmark inventory are in Supplementary Note 1 (Data Acquisition and Benchmark Construction), which lists the query inventories for Hebei and Hong Kong (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 ) alongside the corresponding data sources and characteristics (Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 ). To rigorously assess Neuro-Air and mitigate hallucinations across the entire analytical lifecycle, we score every response against five core criteria: (1) Data Integration and Synthesis (DIS), which assesses the absolute accuracy of empirical data retrieval; (2) Methodological Soundness (MS), which evaluates the contextual appropriateness of the selected analytical models; (3) Technical Implementation Quality (TIQ), which verifies the executable validity of the generated programmatic code; (4) Response Alignment (RA), which measures the comprehensive fulfillment of the user’s initial query; and (5) Faithfulness (FAI), which ensures that all final conclusions are strictly derived from transparent, intermediate computational evidence. The comprehensive performance score is the average of these five criteria. Detailed operational definitions and step-by-step verification protocols are provided in Supplementary Note 2 (Detailed Evaluation Framework and Protocols); the overall 1–10 scoring scale is given in Supplementary Table 5 , and the complete scoring rubric applied by the human experts is provided in Supplementary Note 5 , with the full scale as administered to the panel in Supplementary Table 11 . We apply these criteria through four complementary channels 46 , 59 , 60 , organized around two levels of quality. Execution-level quality, namely data retrieval, computation, and code execution, is captured by the three automated channels; professional-level quality, namely whether a response is dependable enough to inform a real-world air-quality management decision and thus requires environmental judgment that execution accuracy alone cannot capture, is probed by the human panel. (i) A multiple AI-judge evaluation scores all 317 queries on the five criteria using three independent LLM judges (Kimi-K2, Claude 4 Sonnet, Qwen3), each judge scoring every response once, with the final score taken as the mean across the three judges, across the four foundation-model backbones. (ii) A judge-free objective channel grades 90 programmatically verified tasks against ground truth recomputed live from the database (this benchmark is detailed below with the ablation). (iii) Objective process metrics are parsed deterministically from the complete execution logs. (iv) A blinded human calibration study was conducted with 15 active environmental-management professionals, including atmospheric analysts, data engineers, and policymakers. Each evaluator independently scored the responses generated by the baseline Claude 4 Sonnet backbone under the full multi-agent configuration using a holistic 1–10 rubric. Evaluation was performed on a difficulty-weighted subset of 32 queries (11 from Hong Kong and 21 from Hebei) covering all six task categories. The subset was selected by stratified random sampling across task categories, followed by manual review to retain more challenging items. In the fully crossed design, evaluators could inspect the generated code and intermediate execution outputs alongside the final answer, but were blinded to the automated scores; disjoint calibration examples were provided for reference. Because standalone LLM judges can exhibit internal biases 61 , 62 , 63 , the human panel and the judge-free channels serve as independent cross-checks. Full panel composition, recruitment, consent, protocols, rubric, and statistics are provided in Supplementary Note 2 and Methods. The four evaluation backbones (GPT-5, Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3) were accessed under standardized conditions during August 2025 (sampling temperature 0.2, provider default for GPT-5): Claude 4 Sonnet (snapshot claude-sonnet-4-20250514 ) and DeepSeek-V3 (V3-0324) via their official APIs, and GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro through an OpenAI-compatible gateway. The process-metrics log analysis additionally covers Qwen3-235B-A22B and Kimi-K2 (six backbones in total), whereas the architecture ablation below uses a separate set of five more recent backbones (Methods): because the architecture is backbone-agnostic and the available models advanced during the revision, Neuro-Air supports drop-in replacement of updated backbones without modifying the agent workflow. The full set of backbones and judges, and the roles they play, is summarized in Supplementary Table 9 . Finally, we isolate two design choices through matched ablations, varying one factor at a time while keeping the backbone, database, persistent Python runtime, system prompt, execution-step budget, and number of attempts fixed (Methods). The shared step budget limits the number of code executions in each arm, but does not enforce equal overall compute; the additional token cost of the multi-agent configuration is reported separately below. Both ablations are evaluated on a 90-task programmatically verified (PV) subset, for which outputs can be deterministically recomputed from the source data and assessed by an automatic validator without human or LLM-based judging (Fig. 5 ; Methods). For the architecture ablation, we compare the full multi-agent topology with a single-agent configuration in which all roles are merged. Because the worker roles form sequentially dependent stages of the workflow, removing an individual worker would disrupt the pipeline rather than provide a meaningful partial ablation; we therefore use the fully merged configuration as the comparison. For the execution-paradigm ablation, we compare native Python execution with a conventional function-calling workflow. Function calling requires repeated exchanges between the model and external tools during iterative analyses, whereas Neuro-Air generates the analytical procedure as executable Python code and runs it within an isolated sandbox. This reduces repeated communication and token use while keeping numerical operations within a reproducible execution environment. Quantitative performance and comparative analysis The automated evaluation exceeded a 70% aggregate score on every backbone and 85% on three of the four, with GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro scoring highest (both 91.6%, and indistinguishable from one another), ahead of Claude 4 Sonnet (89.0%) and DeepSeek-V3 (79.4%) (Supplementary Fig. 1 ). A complementary standalone-LLM control, which used the Claude 4 Sonnet backbone given only a web-search tool, with no access to the environmental databases or the execution pipeline (117 Hong Kong runs), scored 0.25–0.30 under the same three judges, empirically confirming that the data-integration and execution layers, rather than the underlying language model alone, carry the system’s performance (Supplementary Table 9 ). The three judges (Kimi-K2 64 , Claude 4 Sonnet 39 , Qwen3 65 ) rated each query independently, and their scores were highly consistent (mean inter-rater correlation 0.93, Cronbach’s α = 0.97; Supplementary Fig. 2 ), although they differed systematically in absolute level, with Qwen3 scoring every backbone highest and Claude 4 Sonnet every backbone lowest. To quantify sampling uncertainty, t -based 95% confidence intervals on the per-backbone mean scores are all narrower than ± 1.5 percentage points, indicating that the between-backbone differences are not artifacts of sampling noise. Beyond the judge-based scores, we report objective process metrics derived directly from the execution logs, without human or model-based evaluation. A rule-based parser was applied to 1,902 runs (317 queries × six backbones: the four evaluation models above, Qwen3-235B-A22B, and Kimi-K2). First-attempt code execution succeeded in 99.3% of runs (Wilson 95% CI: 98.8–99.6%). Across all runs, 61 (3.2%) encountered at least one execution error, of which 60 subsequently recovered, and none exhausted the execution-step budget. Among 42,893 salient numerals identified in the final responses, 97.4% (95% CI: 97.3–97.6%) could be traced to executed computational evidence, or 94.2% under strict matching. Median latency was 71 s per query (90th percentile: 247 s), with 96.3% of runs completing within ten minutes. Pollution-transmission queries had the highest error-run rate (8.1%), approximately 2.7 × the corpus average, consistent with the greater computational complexity of source attribution and transport analysis. Of the 76 logged error events, 49 were triggered by security guardrails rather than code failures, corresponding to a non-guardrail code-failure rate of 1.3% of runs. Per-backbone results are reported in Supplementary Table 8 . For Kimi-K2, 29.0% of code blocks lack a recorded execution outcome; its error rates may therefore be underestimated, and the aggregate values should be interpreted accordingly. Excluding Kimi-K2 yields similar results, with a first-attempt execution success rate of 99.1% across the remaining 1585 runs (Wilson 95% CI: 98.5–99.5%). This reliability depends on the execution paradigm itself. On the matched Hong Kong pool, native Python execution attained 99.6% (95% CI 98.7–99.9%) first-attempt success versus 91.4% (84.9–95.3%) for the function-calling baseline (disjoint intervals), with at least one execution error in only 1.7% of native runs versus 45.3% of function-calling runs (a ~ 27 × relative difference); 95.6% of function-calling errors (108 of 113) arose at the SQL/tool interface, versus 8.3% (1 of 12) under native execution on the same pool. As the baseline ran on a single, unrecorded backbone, this contrast is strongly indicative rather than fully factorial. Having established that the execution core is reliable, we next isolate the source of that reliability through a controlled architecture ablation. On the architecture axis, the matched single-agent versus multi-agent comparison ran across five additional backbones spanning four model families and a broad capability range (single-agent accuracy 51–92%): DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GPT-5.5, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen2.5-72B, and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, under one frozen configuration with no per-model tuning. These differ from the evaluation backbones above because the architecture is backbone-agnostic and models advanced during the revision, so the ablation is an independent controlled study (Methods). The multi-agent architecture improved accuracy on every backbone (+3.3 to +10.0 percentage points; Fig. 6 a, c and Table 1 ). Pooled across the 450 paired tasks (the common 90-task benchmark × five backbones), accuracy rose from 82.0% to 88.4%, a +6.4-point gain (exact McNemar p = 2.5 × 10 −5 ; 38 tasks solved only by the multi-agent arm versus 9 only by the single agent). Two backbones were individually significant ( p = 0.031 each, unadjusted); the per-backbone gain intervals of two others span zero, so the effect is carried by the pooled analysis, which a task-level cluster bootstrap confirms (95% CI + 3.6 to + 9.3; Methods). Because the multi-agent arm bundles role specialization, coordination, and the in-loop auditing pass, this comparison evaluates the complete pipeline rather than independently isolating the causal contribution of each architectural component (Methods).
